summary: Most UK mid-air collisions happen in good VMC at low level and about half near aerodromes. The big sky helps as much as see-and-avoid. Keep your eyes inside the cockpit no more than 25% of the time, scan in short 10° steps pausing at least a second, randomise levels, avoid choke points and final approach tracks, and use lights and electronic conspicuity (ADS-B on 1090 MHz is the preferred UK system). Built from the Skyway Code pp.129-132.
src: The Skyway Code (CAP 1535 v4, Nov 2023), pp.129-132
sections: The risk
More than 100 airproxes are reported to the UK Airprox Board each year
Almost all mid-air collisions are in good VMC at relatively low level and around half happen near aerodromes, many in the circuit
No pilot detects 100% of traffic, especially outside the normal field of view
Mitigations
Avoid choke points at beacons and VRPs and avoid direct overflight
Avoid gliding sites. Gliders thermal in groups and fly cross-country downwind. Note cable launch heights
Hang glider and paraglider sites may not be on charts and may be activated by NOTAM
Randomise cruising levels, for example 2,200 ft instead of 2,000 ft
Avoid crossing the final approach track of aerodromes outside CAS, even outside the ATZ. Feathered arrows on charts show instrument approach paths, descending at about 300 ft per NM
Know joining and circuit procedures. Be clear on position and intentions on the radio
The visual scan
Keep a clean windscreen
Eyes inside the cockpit no more than 25% of the time
Move your eyes in steps of about 10°, pausing at least 1 second. The eyes struggle to detect movement while the head is moving
Side-to-side method: start at far left and sweep right pausing in each block, then check the panel
Front-to-side method: start in the centre, move left, swing back to the centre, then go right, then check the panel
Do not fixate inside: look out every few seconds. A passenger can help if briefed
Electronic and visual conspicuity
Electronic conspicuity (EC) lets aircraft be detected by ATC or other aircraft. The transponder is the most common device
ADS-B broadcasts GPS position (Out) for receivers (In). The CAA preferred national system is ADS-B at 1090 MHz. FLARM and PilotAware use other bands to transmit
EC devices are not always interoperable and must not replace a good lookout
Strobes and anti-collision beacons on at all times after entering the runway environment. Landing lights on approaching an aerodrome and in high traffic density
Black aircraft can show up well, while white or broken patterns blend into grey backgrounds

sum.Mitigations: Choke points, random levels and final approach tracks.
sum.The visual scan: 25% inside, 10° steps and two scan methods.

cards.q: How many airproxes are reported each year?
Where do about half of UK mid-air collisions happen?
cards.a: Near aerodromes, many in the circuit.

cards.q: Maximum time eyes inside the cockpit?
Minimum pause for each scan step?

cards.a: Many pilots use them, so randomising reduces conflict risk.

cards.q: Descent along an instrument approach path?

cards.a: Electronic conspicuity: technology detecting aircraft position electronically.

cards.q: When should strobes and beacons be on?
cards.a: At all times after entering the runway environment.

cards.q: When should landing lights be on?
cards.a: On approaching an aerodrome and in areas of high traffic density.

quiz.q: Eyes should be inside the cockpit for no more than:
quiz.why: The rest of the time look outside.

o: In good VMC at low level
quiz.why: Traffic density is higher at low level.

quiz.q: The CAA preferred UK ADS-B frequency is:
quiz.why: ADS-B on 1090 MHz is the preferred national system.

quiz.q: Which statement about gliders is correct?
o: They may congregate in thermals and fly cross-country
They always stay overhead their launch site
They never use cable launches, only aerotows
They never operate from sites not shown on charts
quiz.why: Gliders do not confine themselves to the site.

quiz.q: An effective scan moves the eyes in steps of about:
quiz.why: 10° steps with a pause of at least a second each.
